title: What is known about 1RB0RE_0RC0RF_1LD1RA_1RE0LD_0LB1RC_1LE---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_0RC0RF_1LD1RA_1RE0LD_0LB1RC_1LE---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a fast counter (the last block, +4 per round, rounds doubling) and a slow list of blocks crossed by one walker per round; when a walker reaches the left end the list is rebuilt longer. Three rebuilds have been seen, the last at step 2.3·1010; their general rule is not known, so the run cannot be followed further.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 189 cells have been visited and 86 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Three rounds of the run, for any tape further left
claims.text: Three consecutive rounds of the run from blank tape (between moments the head is in C on the first 0 right of everything written), each proved for every tape left of the cells it visits, with its exact step count.

claims.title: No halt in 3·10<sup>10</sup> steps; three rebuilds
claims.text: Direct simulation for 3·10<sup>10</sup> steps. At the moments the head is in C on the first 0 right of everything written the tape is a list of blocks of 1s separated by single 0s; the last block grows by 4 per round; in walking phases the rounds satisfy T′ = 2T + 4 exactly. Rebuilds of the list at steps 72,083, 11,004,261 and 22,558,329,283 (the table).

claims.title: Walkers and rebuilds
claims.text: Outside rebuilds, each round moves one walker one block to the left (2 5 → 5 2 or 2 x → x+3); a rebuild happens when a walker reaches the leading 3, and lengthens the list of 2s (13, then 26 blocks). Seen in all 116 sample moments of the first 3·1010 steps; not shown for all sizes.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. See the heuristic claims above for what a halt would need.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine is a two-level counter: its last block of 1s grows by four per round, each round twice as long as the one before, while a walker crosses the list of blocks on its left one block per round. When the walker arrives, the list is rebuilt longer. This page runs the machine and shows the rounds.

facts.text: No halt; three rebuilds of the list seen.
Rounds of the run proved in Lean for any tape further left.

sections.heading: A fast counter and a slow list
html: Each time the head is in state C on the first blank cell right of everything written, the tape is a list of blocks of 1s separated by single 0s (2^6 below is six blocks of length 2). The last block is a fast counter: it grows by 4 in each round (a round is the stretch between two such moments, taken every second one), and each round takes exactly twice as long as the one before plus 4 steps once the list is in a walking phase. All the other blocks have length 2 mod 3 except the leading 3 or 6; in each round exactly one thing happens in this slow list: a walker moves one block to the left.

Two kinds of walkers appear: a 5 that swaps with the 2 on its left (2 5 → 5 2, the 0 between them moves three cells) and a block that swallows the 2 on its left and grows by 3 (2 x → x+3). When a walker reaches the leading 3, the list is rebuilt: the leading block becomes 6, then the next round turns the fast counter's cells into a much longer list of 2s and restarts the walk. Rebuild 2 left 13 blocks of 2 to cross, rebuild 3 left 26; each crossing costs one doubling round per block, so the phases grow like iterated exponentials: rebuilds at about 7·104, 1.1·107 and 2.3·1010 steps, and the next one not before about 213·2.8·1010 ≈ 2·1014 steps (13 more blocks for the growing walker), likely much later.

sections.heading: Why it is hard to settle
html: The machine halts only in state F reading a 1. Walking rounds are regular (three of them are proved in Lean for every tape further left), but whether a halt can happen depends on the rebuilds, which come exponentially rarely and whose rule is not known for all sizes. Under the observed pattern each rebuild only makes the list longer, which would make the machine run forever, but this is an extrapolation from three rebuilds.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.04).
After 109 steps the tape spans 189 cells (10 left of the start, 174 right), with a density of 1s of 0.455.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

summary: Two-level counter: the last block grows by 4 per round in doubling time while a walker crosses a list of 2s; rebuilds at 7e4, 1.1e7, 2.3e10 steps lengthen the list; open.
